utterances.text: At the entrance there were -- there was a staff and the kitchen in the same building. Then the second building was the prison, sir, where people were detained, were beaten up, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Witness, what you're saying -- what you said here was that you saw when these people, these -- all of these people, five people, were brought to that headquarters area. Not from another building. You saw when they were first brought in, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In my opinion, the children were kept there for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You said nothing in this paragraph, nothing in this statement, about the children, as you call them, the young people, being brought from the cellar, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not saying they were children just to say this, but they were children, in fact. This is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Witness, you heard the question. Please don't avoid it. You said nothing about them being brought from the cellar, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I understand what is the dispute here, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, absolutely. The plain meaning of the words here, the plain meaning of the witness's words, is that he claims to have been present already in Jabllanice when these five people were actually brought to Jabllanice. That is the plain meaning of his words --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But read -- read the entire paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me tell you, let's listen to what this witness is saying. He said "During our stay in the headquarters in Jabllanice, we witnessed how one Serb, three Romas, and one Albanian man were brought into the headquarters." Carry on. "They were ordered to serve the commanders with tea and something to eat. I could observe that they had all -- they had all -- they all had been beaten very badly, and when they brought them into the headquarters they handled them very roughly." These are people who are already in the -- in the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot confirm that, and I don't think Your Honour can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: No, but the witness has said this. And that's a matter of whether you accept what the witness is saying. Obviously you're the judges of fact. What I -- what I read this to mean, and I will be very plain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: How I read this and interpret it is that the witness is saying he saw them brought to the headquarters area. The whole -- the place that he has described as the headquarters - please, let me just finish - and that they had already been beaten before they got there. Now, you know that the witness claims that he has information -- or that he (redacted). He claims to have been there. He claims to have been here. He claims to have seen everything. My point is that the plain meaning of this paragraph as I read it, and I may be the only one who sees this reading of it, is that he saw them when they were first brought to Jabllanice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But in the meantime, Mr. Harvey, the question you have about this and the way you read it, the witness has clearly answered that question. And he says they came not from outside the headquarters area, they came from one building to another. Which is the -- which is the way Judge Moloto and, for that matter, I read it. So shouldn't you go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Well, I was going on. In fact, the question I was asking in which the witness, in my submission, was avoiding answering, was that at no stage in this statement does he claim that those people were in the cellar, were being brought from the cellar. Which is what he is saying now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Witness, it's correct, isn't it, that you did not say that those people were brought from the cellar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, you asked me where they were brought from. I said they were brought from the cellar when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: In your statement you say nothing about them being in the cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Please, I -- I'm sorry I really --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: -- may I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: -- do insist on an answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: May I object. We've been over and over and over this point, and it must be clear that we have exhausted it. And I would ask that Your Honours direct that the case move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Harvey, will you move on, please. The statement tells us where the people were brought to. It doesn't tell us where they were brought from. That's what the statement says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I accept that -- [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So let's move on, sir. Yes, we can accept that he never said in the statement where they were brought from, but he told us where they were brought to. It stands to reason. We see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we can move on. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I can accept that that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm about to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Is that a serious answer, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is a serious answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Very well. You were on good terms with Lahi Brahimaj after the war, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You spent time together with him in Albania, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have photographs with him when he invited me for dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Photographs of you smiling in a group together; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You can smile even if you are under pressure, because of the words he said to me and how my life -- what -- how my life developed after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And you took money to help his nephew get to Italy, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Sorry, we are in private session. This is clearly something that can be answered in open session, I think. May we go into open session, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is no lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: But my question, Witness, was: You took money to help Lahi's nephew get to Italy, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. In the situation I was, I couldn't do anything to take his nephew to Italy. I was not in that position. If I was, I would have taken my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I'm suggesting that was in approximately December of 1998. That was when you were having dinner together with him in Tirana, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can show you also the hotel they invited me to and I was obliged to go. They called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Even after the war, in 1999, you were on good terms with the KLA and with Lahi Brahimaj, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: KLA is a very large organisation. Perhaps it can just be expressed to a single individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- and I don't know how he becomes friends with KLA as a -- which is not a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You joined a celebration on Flag Day, that's the 28th of November, 1999, didn't you, in Peje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Do you have any proof of that? It is true that I took part in the celebrations on the occasion of the Flag's Day. I do it every year as an Albanian. But I don't recall when.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: As long as you agree that you were present at a KLA celebration of Flag Day in November of 1999. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That celebration was staged by the government of Kosova, not by the KLA. It was the Kosova government. And in every such rally, I have taken part.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. I think that's a convenient moment. It may well be that I won't have any more questions. If I do, it will just be one or two. But I'd just like a moment to reflect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're giving you a moment to reflect. Will you please reflect and come back to us. We want to know whether you still have questions or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll take the four minutes and then we can start again. I'll take the four minutes. I'll take every second I can get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. I'd like to see if there are a couple of things that we can agree about in the remaining time that we have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could we go back to -- this will be tab 1, which will be 0346 for Your Honours, paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Paragraph 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have that in front you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the sake of record: It's 03046.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the paragraph that we've just been discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: There go my four minutes. I hoped to get three questions, but I only got one. But, it's better than nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Better than nothing. By which you mean? You still have two more questions to ask later? Okay. Once again, Mr. Witness, we've come to the end of our working day. We're still not done with you. You still have to come back tomorrow. I remind you once again ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we excuse you, there's something that we need to do that might affect tomorrow's time, so you stay there for a while longer. Do the parties have anything to say about scheduling for tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. We are confident that we will conclude to enable Mr. Rogers to close the Prosecution case before we rise tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What about starting time tomorrow? Do you have anything to say on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to start as early as practicable, considering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, okay. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- concerning some of the concerns that I've heard. I'm happy to start any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me say what messages have been passed on to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've been alerted to a possible request that we start at 8.00 tomorrow because we want to cover time lost today, and then I thought the parties were going to make representations on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no difficulty with that. We didn't know how long Mr. Harvey would be, whether he would conclude today. So with that in mind, we anticipated we may need a little longer than perhaps necessary. I don't know how long Mr. Guy-Smith thinks he's going to be. I think we're really in his hands. Because I will be very short. I don't know what Mr. Emmerson's planning to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How short is short going to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I'm not going to hold myself to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: It will be short, not long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, part of the reason that I wanted to do what we did today as an experiment dealing with a relatively easy question was to get some kind of a sense or a feeling for how long things would take. I have structured the examination in such a fashion that most of the questions to be asked are sufficiently, I think, straightforward and clear and easy to follow, that if we have an honest give and flow in terms of question and answer, I could get done starting at 9.00. My concerns, however, are seeing what happened in the brief four minutes that we just had, that we may need a bit more time. So I would suggest we start -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've got a feeling now in the four minutes. Can you give us a straightforward clear answer how much time you think you will need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that I will need at least two sessions and probably two and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you still want to start at 8.00? It looks like you're the one who wanted to start at 8.00, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... to rush out of bed for 8.00, but we will if we think we need it. I don't know what Mr. Emmerson thinks his time will be, but I'm happy to come early.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think -- I think, based on discusses with Mr. Rogers, that on the state of the evidence so far, half a session would be sufficient to deal with Mr. Rogers and any questions that I may have. Is that -- I mean, unless Mr. Rogers dissents from that. That means that as matters currently stand, unless there's a significant change over the next -- during the course of Mr. Guy-Smith's cross-examination, he ought to be in a position to have two and a half sessions sitting at 9.00. We have three sessions altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. And if he has two and a half, and the remaining half you two will share.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And we'll finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: On the current state of the evidence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think what Mr. Emmerson is suggesting, that as the evidence has thus far been presented, and having some appreciation of where I am going - and I think he has a good appreciation of where I'm going - that based upon the current state of the evidence as between Mr. Rogers and Mr. Emmerson, they can finish what they need to do in a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Half a session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Half a session. I'm sorry, half a session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... the only question is, is whether he -- in the unlikely event that there's a change of course either by myself or Mr. Rogers arising out of Mr. Guy-Smith's cross-examination, the only question is whether the Court, out of an abundance of caution, will want to sit an hour early because there's a possibility that things might change. I can't guarantee they won't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I was going to suggest that we do that so that we have some little fat -- a buffer, because if we don't do that and we need to sit longer tomorrow, then there's no way we can do it. So, that being the case, we are going to adjourn to 8.00 tomorrow morning, if everybody else is listening. Is that okay? Good. Now, can I come back to you, Mr. Witness. We will start at 8.00 instead of 9.00 tomorrow morning, okay? If you can just wake up just one hour earlier and that will be the last day, hopefully.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't mind that, Your Honour. But I have a question. Shall I bring these papers, these documents with me tomorrow? I brought these two cards with me when he said to me yesterday that you haven't been in a -- a member of the KLA. These are the documents that I have with me to show that I have been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your Honour has got a microphone on, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, we couldn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I asked the witness to bring the documents that shows -- show that he is a member of the KLA or was a member of the KLA tomorrow, together with the documents that he's promised today to bring because it is now late in the evening, particularly for you people there, to start looking at the documents here and now. Okay? So bring those documents tomorrow and bring the documents that you were asking me about a few minutes ago tomorrow as well. We can look at them tomorrow. Having said that, again I remind you that you may not discuss the case with anybody until you are finally excused from further testimony. See you tomorrow at 8.00 in the morning. I beg your pardon. May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We are adjourned to tomorrow morning, 8.00, same place. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 20th day (redacted).
